rows.text: Honestly, easier than I expected for a first pass. The Module 1 checklist told me exactly what Health Canada expects (8 required leaves, bilingual flags on the PM and labelling), progress ticked 0 to 100 percent, and the generate/upload affordances meant I wasn't hunting for where things go. The one place I paused was the placeholder-ID block, but that's correct friction, not confusion, and the Rename step cleared it in one action. Doing this in Vault or docuBridge, the equivalent would have taken me longer and more clicks.

Genuinely smooth. The Module 1 checklist drove me straight through eight leaves with a live 0/8 progress counter, generate-or-upload on each, and the bilingual EN/FR handling on 1.3.1 and 1.3.3 was correct without me fighting it. The placeholder-to-real Dossier ID rename, the sequence 0001 replace, the e-sign and verify were all a couple of clicks each. The only real friction is conceptual, not mechanical: a first-timer needs to understand REP, lifecycle replace ops, and SoD to know why each step matters — but for someone who files eCTD, this was the least fiddly tooling I've touched.

Honestly, this went about as smoothly as I've ever had an eCTD flow go. The Module 1 checklist drove me straight down the 8 required leaves with progress ticking 12/25/38%, generate-or-upload right where I'd expect, and bilingual 1.3.1/1.3.3 correctly demanding EN+FR. Rename to re-key the placeholder, open seq 0001, drop a replace leaf — all the things that are fiddly and error-prone in eCTD Office were a couple of clicks. The one bit of friction is real-world sequencing: the placeholder-ID block means you can't get a clean run until REP issues the Dossier ID, which is correct but is a wait outside the tool.

Genuinely smooth. The Module 1 checklist drove me — 8 required leaves, progress ticking 0 to 100%, generate-or-upload per section, bilingual EN+FR handled on 1.3.1/1.3.3 without me fighting it. The placeholder-ID block, the rename, the re-validate, the export, the e-sign and verify all chained the way I'd actually work a sequence. Re-authoring 4 leaves to clear the PDF/A noise and spinning up 0001 as a replace were both one call each. This is less friction than eCTD Office plus GlobalSubmit for a Module 1 CS-BE.

Honestly, easier than I expected for something this regulatory. The Module 1 checklist told me exactly which 8 documents I needed and ticked from 0% to 100% as I filled each one, and the generate buttons did the boring cover-letter and application-form drafting for me. The part that made me nervous was the placeholder-ID validation failure and the 409 export block, but the message literally told me the fix (file a Dossier ID Request in REP, then Rename), so after re-keying to e478210 it just cleared and exported. The e-sign, verify, and lifecycle-0001 replace all worked without me guessing.

Honestly easier than I expected. The Module 1 checklist walked me through all 8 required docs with a live 0/8 progress bar, and the generate buttons filled the cover letter, application form, attestation, Form V and CS-BE straight from the company details, so I only had to upload the PDFs I actually had. The one place I paused was the placeholder-ID block at export, but the message literally told me to file a REP Dossier ID Request and then Rename to the real ID, so I knew exactly what to do. The e-sign and lifecycle-replace steps sound scary in the abstract but here they were just one action each with clear responses.

Honestly, easier than I expected for a task this heavy. The Module 1 checklist told me exactly what eight documents I owed and ticked up a percentage as I filled each one, so I never wondered if I'd missed a leaf. The one spot I'd have paused is the placeholder-to-real Dossier ID rename — I had to go get the real HC ID and re-key it — but the validator and the export block flat-out told me that was the reason, so at least I wasn't guessing. Forty steps is a lot, but each one gave me a clear result, and I never hit a dead end or an unexplained error.

Honestly, easier than my current SOP-and-Acrobat grind. The module checklist told me exactly what 8 Module 1 leaves I needed and ticked up 0 to 100% as I filled them, generate-or-upload was obvious, and the bilingual sections took both EN and FR without me fighting it. The two hard moments were the ones that SHOULD be hard - the placeholder-ID block and the signer-is-author block - and both handed me the exact next step, so I never had to guess what "fix it" meant.

Honestly easier than my usual eValidator-plus-checklist grind. The Module 1 checklist drove me through all eight required leaves with a live 0/8 to 8/8 counter, the placeholder-ID block told me exactly what to do (file the REP request, then Rename), and after re-keying to e478210 everything just carried over. The only friction was cognitive, not mechanical: I had to keep straight which sequence was active during the 0001 replace and re-author, but the current-view and outline calls resolved that in seconds.

Honestly, easier than I expected for a task this heavy. Module 1 filled to 100% with a clear 0/8 to 8/8 progress counter, the placeholder-ID block gave me the exact rule (CA-REP-0001) and the fix path (REP request then Rename), and re-validate cleared it immediately. The one friction point is that the real trust-building steps — enforced SoD, PDF/A-1b regeneration, the pre-flight report — are deep in the flow across two dossiers and a workspace toggle; a first-timer would need someone to point them at those, they don't surface on their own.

Honestly, easier than I expected for something this regulated. The Module 1 checklist walked me through all 8 required leaves with progress ticking to 100%, generate-or-upload on each, and the bilingual EN+FR sections were handled without me guessing. The one real friction was the placeholder-to-real Dossier ID dance — export slammed shut at 409 and I had to go do the REP rename before it cleared — but that friction is the point, and it was one obvious step, not a maze. By the time I hit the follow-up 0001 replace and the consolidated pre-flight report, I was moving fast.

Honestly, easier than I expected for something this regulated. I built all 8 Module 1 leaves, hit the export block, re-keyed the placeholder ID, and got a real 11KB zip out the other side without ever guessing what to do next — the progress bar (0/8 to 8/8) and the 409 block told me exactly where I stood. The one part that isn't self-serve is that I still have to go do the real REP Dossier-ID Request and the actual HC eValidator run outside the tool, but the tool was upfront that those are mine to do, so I didn't waste time expecting it to file for me.

Honestly, this went smoothly for someone who does this daily — Module 1 filled leaf by leaf with clear 12/25/38% progress, the bilingual 1.3.1/1.3.3 took both EN and FR without a fight, and the placeholder-to-real rename carried all the content over. The one place I braced for pain — the export — is exactly where it behaved: it 409'd on the placeholder, I fixed the Dossier ID, and it cleared. The SoD, e-sign, and lifecycle-replace steps were each a single obvious action. Nothing made me hunt.

Honestly, this was smooth in a way I don't expect from a v1 tool. The Module 1 checklist tracked to 8/8 with a live percent, generate-or-upload was obvious per leaf, and the bilingual EN+FR slots on 1.3.1/1.3.3 were handled the way HC's regional backbone actually wants. The one place I sat up was the 409 export block on the placeholder ID — but rename to e478210, re-validate, re-export cleared it in three moves, and the lifecycle replace in 0001 just worked. As a publisher this is materially less friction than assembling a sequence in docuBridge by hand.

Honestly easier than I expected for something this regulated — the Module 1 checklist gave me a clear 0/8 to 100% progress bar, generate-or-upload on each leaf, and I never had to guess the eCTD folder structure. The only real friction was conceptual, not mechanical: the placeholder-ID rename, the two sign paths, and the workspace SoD toggle are a lot of moving parts, and as a coordinator who doesn't author I'd need the run-book once before I'd fly it solo. But no dead ends, no cryptic failures — every step landed.

Honestly, easier than I expected for something this heavy. The Module 1 checklist counting me up 12%, 25%, 50%... to 100% is exactly the progress signal I live on in Smartsheet, so I always knew where I stood. The one place I'd want a hand is the placeholder-to-real Dossier ID step — I get why it blocks, but a first-timer needs to understand REP/CESG is out-of-band; the tool told me, but it's a real-world dependency, not a click. The re-run TIER-3 stretch (re-authoring for PDF/A, toggling the SoD policy) was more steps than a coordinator would do daily, but each one landed cleanly.

Honestly, easier than I feared for something this regulated. The Module 1 checklist told me exactly what eight leaves I needed and ticked up 12%, 25%, 38%... so I always knew where I stood, and the bilingual sections took both my EN and FR product monograph files without a fight. The one real snag was the placeholder-ID block at export, but even that told me precisely what to do (file the REP request, then Rename to the real ID), and once I re-keyed to e478210 it just cleared. The later SoD and PDF/A steps were more concept-heavy, but each one was a single call with a plain-language result.

Honestly easier than my usual Word-template-plus-XML-tool slog. The Module 1 checklist told me exactly the 8 leaves I owe, filled the progress bar as I went, and the bilingual PM and Labelling sections took EN and FR together without me hand-editing an index. The one real friction was intended: the placeholder ID validation failure at step 11 and the hard export block at step 12 stopped me cold, but the Rename to the real HC ID cleared it in one move and everything carried over. Re-authoring the four leaves as PDF/A-1b and then seeing the advisories drop from 12 to 10 was frictionless.

Honestly, easier than I expected for an old paper-and-binder man. The Module 1 checklist counted me up 0-of-8 to 100% and I always knew what was left, and when the export slammed shut with that 409 I wasn't lost — it told me the exact finding and what to do. The one part I'd have fumbled cold is the placeholder-to-real Dossier-ID rename and the REP request order, but the tool spelled out the four CESG/WebTrader steps, so I got through it.

Honestly, easier than I braced for. The Module 1 checklist did the remembering for me — eight required leaves, a progress count, and I just filled each one until it hit 100%. When export slammed shut with that 409 I thought I'd broken it, but it told me plainly it was the placeholder ID, I did the Rename, re-validated, and it went straight through. Re-keying a whole dossier and having every leaf carry over unchanged is the kind of thing that used to cost me an afternoon and a nervous phone call.

Genuinely smooth end-to-end. The guided Module 1 checklist (8 leaves, live 0-100% progress) meant I never guessed what was missing, generate-vs-upload was one click each, and the placeholder-to-real Dossier ID re-key carried all content over without re-placing anything. The lifecycle replace into seq 0001 and the enforced-SoD block both "just worked" on the first try, which for a Part-11 flow is rare — I got to a signed, validated package without touching a config file or a manual.

Genuinely smooth. Eight Module 1 leaves via a mix of generate and upload, then validate/export/sign/verify were each one call with an unambiguous status. The one point of real friction — the placeholder-ID export block — is exactly the friction I want; the Rename to the real HC ID cleared it and the content carried over, so nothing had to be re-placed. The bilingual 1.3.1/1.3.3 handling (EN+FR both attached before the leaf turned complete) matched how I actually file.

Honestly, easier than I feared for someone who has never touched eCTD. The Module 1 checklist told me exactly which 8 documents I needed, gave me generate-or-upload for each, and ticked me up a percentage as I went, so I was never guessing what was left. Where it got real was the export getting slapped with a 409 block over the placeholder ID — I had to go file the REP request, re-key to the real Dossier ID, and re-validate before it would let me out, and the enforced signer-is-author rejection (422) made me stop and get a distinct approver. Those were the moments that felt like actual regulatory work, not clicks, but the path through each was spelled out.

Genuinely manageable, even for someone like me with zero eCTD muscle memory. The Module 1 checklist counted me up 0/8 to 100%, the tool generated the forms I'd have panicked over authoring, and the placeholder-to-real Dossier-ID rename was one step. The one thing I did NOT have to think about was chasing PDF/A noise across every leaf — re-generating 1.0/1.2.3/1.2.4/1.6 wiped those advisories at the source, and the consolidated pre-flight report at the end meant I didn't have to re-run validate seven times to hand QA a clean picture.

Very clear at almost every step. Rule IDs like CA-REP-0001 and CA-W-7006 map to how I actually read validation output, the messages told me the fix ("file a Dossier ID Request through REP, then set the real ID"), and the export 409 said "validation_not_passed" with the exact blocking finding rather than a vague error. The SoD result reading separated/conflict/conflicting_authors in plain language was unusually legible. The only thing I had to read twice was the distinction between the PDF/A-1b advisory warnings and a hard defect, but the report spelled that out.

At every step the system told me exactly what it did and, more importantly, what it did NOT do. Validation came back with real rule IDs (CA-REP-0001, CA-W-7006/7008) and per-leaf messages I could act on, not a vague red X. The 409 export block spelled out the blocking finding and my two options (fix or reasoned override). What impressed me most was the honesty framing: the eValidator result is labeled user-attested-external with an explicit note that the tool did not run HC's validator, and the e-sign is called Part-11 aligned, not certified. I never had to guess what a green checkmark actually meant.

Very clear the whole way — every state change told me exactly what happened and why. The 409 export block literally handed me the blocking rule ['CA-REP-0001'] with the fix ("file a REP request, then Rename"), and I watched it flip to a 200 with X-Export-Validation=passed once I set the real ID. The PDF/A advisories name the leaf, the rule ID (CA-W-7006/7008), and what PDF/A-1b would require; the SoD result spells out separated/conflict/authorship_known in plain terms. The current-view and outline showing operation=replace with the modified_leaf back-pointer is exactly the relationship an HC reviewer replays — I didn't have to guess.

At every step I knew what the system was telling me. The validator names its version and sync (v1.2, HC criteria v5.3), gives real rule IDs (CA-REP-0001, CA-W-7006/7008) with the offending leaf, and the 409 export block spelled out the exact blocking finding instead of handing me a bad zip. The lifecycle view showing operation=replace with modified_leaf back-pointer is exactly what I inspect before I trust a supersede. The one thing I'd flag: the preflight report shows signature_verified=false and the SoD conflict signer as the "current" esign state — a QA reader could misread that snapshot, so I'd want the report to show the last GOOD signature, not the last attempted one.

Very clear, and that surprised me because I'm still learning HC terminology. Every finding had a real rule ID (CA-REP-0001, CA-W-7006/7008) and a plain-English explanation, so I could copy the rule ID to a senior instead of hand-waving. The one thing I'd have wanted spelled out more is the PDF/A warnings — 12 of them scared me at first until I read that they're advisory and the submission still PASSES; a junior could easily misread that as "my file is broken." The two-signal validation view (structural PASS next to the attested eValidator PASS) was clear once I read it, but it took me a second to understand ANDS didn't run eValidator itself.

Very clear at almost every step. The validation report gave me real rule IDs (CA-REP-0001 for the placeholder, CA-W-7006/7008 for the PDF/A warnings) instead of a vague "something's wrong," so I could tell my senior precisely what was blocking us. I especially liked that the report separates the structural PASS from the "HC eValidator: PASS (user attested external)" line, and that the export block spells out the exact blocking finding rather than handing me a broken file. The only terms I'd still have to look up are things like OutputIntent and PDF/A-1b, but the messages explain enough that I wasn't lost.

Very clear, and clear in the way I care about — every check named a rule ID (CA-REP-0001, CA-W-7006/7008) and told me the leaf it was about. When export came back 409 it didn't just fail, it said 'validation_not_passed' and listed the exact blocking finding, so I knew precisely what to fix. The one thing I had to read twice was the difference between the structural pass and the PDF/A advisories — but the report is explicit that a plain PDF isn't a hard defect and shows which residual advisories are on files I uploaded versus what the tool now generates clean, so it resolved itself.

Very clear at nearly every step. The validation report gave me real rule IDs (CA-REP-0001, CA-W-7006/7008), a named validator version, and a plain-English message per finding - that's the language I already read in eValidator output, so I knew what I was looking at. The one place I had to slow down was the two SoD signatures in steps 27-28 that only WARN (enforced=false) versus the workspace-policy ones later that actually hard-block (422); a first-timer could conflate "flagged" with "prevented," and I'd want the UI to make that distinction loud.

At almost every step I knew what the system was telling me because it spoke in the rule vocabulary I already use — CA-REP-0001, CA-W-7006/7008, real leaf names, operation='replace' with a modified_leaf back-pointer. The 409 export block naming the exact blocking finding, and the PDF/A advisories counting down 12 to 10 with the residual ones flagged as MY uploads, left zero ambiguity. The one thing I had to read twice was the SoD story arc — warned vs. enforced across two dossiers — but the enforced 422 and the workspace_policy source in the ledger made the distinction crisp.

At almost every step the system told me plainly what it was and wasn't. Rule IDs on every finding, a validator that names its version and what it does NOT check, and a fail-closed 409 that showed me the blocking finding instead of a misleading download — that is exactly the language I use in my own checklists. The only place I had to think was the difference between the earlier ADVISORY SoD warning (steps 27-28) and the later ENFORCED workspace hard-block (37); it's a meaningful distinction but the UI would need to make clear to a filer that a warning alone does not stop them.

At almost every step I knew exactly what the system was telling me because it spoke in real rule IDs, not vibes — CA-REP-0001 for the placeholder block, CA-W-7006/7008 for the PDF/A advisories, HTTP 409 'validation_not_passed', HTTP 422 'segregation_of_duties'. When export blocked, it showed me the exact finding instead of a dead button. The SoD story was crystal: it named the author, named the signer, and told me why signing as the author is a Part-11 weakness. The only thing I had to slow down and read twice was the difference between the structural check passing and the PDF/A advisories staying — but the tool actually spelled that out ('still PASSED, a plain PDF is not a hard defect').

Very clear at every gate — this is the tool's biggest strength for someone like me with no regulatory background. When export failed it named the exact rule (CA-REP-0001) and told me in plain English to file a Dossier ID Request and Rename before filing; the validation report even lists what it does NOT check. The only thing I had to sit with was the PDF/A advisories: 12 CA-W-7006/7008 warnings looked alarming until I read that they're advisory-only and that after re-generating, the ones that remained belong only to PDFs I uploaded, not ones the tool wrote. That distinction was well-explained but took a careful read.

Very clear at every step, and clear in the way that matters to me — findings came back with real rule IDs (CA-REP-0001, CA-W-7006/7008), leaf-level attribution, and a criteria block that names the version and what's checked vs not checked. When export blocked, it told me the exact blocking rule instead of a vague error. The replace op showed operation='replace' with the modified_leaf back-pointer, which is precisely the relationship an HC reviewer replays — I didn't have to guess whether it filed a supersede or a duplicate.

Very clear, and clear in the right currency: rule IDs. CA-REP-0001 told me exactly why export was blocked and exactly what to do (REP Dossier ID Request, then Rename), and CA-W-7006/7008 named the PDF/A gaps at the leaf level. The current-view and the 0001 outline showing operation='replace' with modified_leaf back-pointing to m1-0-1-cover-letter is precisely the relationship I trace in an outline before I transmit — I could read the lifecycle without guessing. The consolidated pre-flight report at the end was the clarity payoff: one artifact with every signal and every caveat inline.

At almost every step I knew what the system was telling me, which is rare for compliance tooling. The validation report with actual rule IDs (CA-REP-0001, CA-W-7006/7008) and the 409 export block that named the exact blocking finding instead of handing me a broken download — that is exactly the kind of "who is blocked and why" signal I live in Smartsheet for. The one place I paused was the SoD story: warned-only in one dossier, hard-blocked (422) in another because of a workspace policy — I had to read carefully to see it was the tenant toggle, not me, driving the difference.

Very clear at nearly every step. When export got blocked with a 409 it didn't just fail — it named CA-REP-0001 and told me exactly what to fix, and I watched it clear on re-validate. The two-signal validation view (structural PASSED next to 'HC eValidator: PASS — user attested external') is the kind of unambiguous status I can drop into a filing tracker without a footnote. The only thing I had to slow down and read was the difference between the tool's structural check and the real eValidator — but that distinction is stated everywhere, so it's honest, not confusing.

Very clear, and in the way that matters to me — every finding carried a rule ID (CA-REP-0001, CA-W-7006, CA-W-7008) and a leaf name, so I could act instead of guess. The disclaimers were blunt and constant: "this is NOT Health Canada's official eValidator," "we do NOT transmit to HC," which is exactly the honesty I want from a tool I'd stake a filing on. I especially liked that the two validation signals stayed separate — the structural PASS never got quietly merged with my attested eValidator result. The only place I had to read twice was the PDF/A advisory story (which PDFs were tool-authored vs. uploaded), but the report spelled out the residual leaves were my own uploads.

Very clear at nearly every step because the messages carry rule IDs I can act on — CA-REP-0001 told me plainly it was a placeholder ID and to file a REP request then Rename, and CA-W-7006/7008 named the exact document and what PDF/A-1b wants. The export 409 didn't just fail, it echoed the blocking finding instead of handing me a misleading download. The one thing I had to read twice was the residual PDF/A advisories after re-generation — it was clear once I saw they belonged only to the five PDFs I uploaded, not the ones the tool authored, but a first-time user might think the fix didn't fully work.

Very clear, and that surprised me. Every screen told me what it was AND what it wasn't — the validator kept saying "structural only, this is NOT Health Canada's eValidator," and the rule IDs like CA-REP-0001 and CA-W-7006 gave me something real to look up. The PDF/A advisories vs. hard blocks were distinguished properly, so I never confused a "you should" with a "you must."

At every stop I knew what the machine was telling me, which is not something I say about software. The validation report gave me real rule IDs — CA-REP-0001, CA-W-7006 — not a spinning wheel, so I could see exactly what was blocking versus what was merely advisory. The one thing I had to read twice was the difference between the structural pass and those PDF/A advisories; it took me a moment to trust that "PASSED with 12 warnings" was genuinely fine and not a trap.

At every step the system told me exactly where I stood: rule IDs on findings (CA-REP-0001, CA-W-7006/7008), the 409 naming the precise blocking finding rather than a dead download, and the 422 SoD block quoting the tenant policy it consulted. The one thing I had to read twice was the PDF/A story — 12 advisories dropping to 10, with the residual explicitly pinned to files I uploaded vs. leaves the tool authored — but once I saw the per-leaf breakdown it was crystal clear and, frankly, more honest than most tools bother to be.

Clear at every step, and unusually so where it matters. The 409 didn't just fail — it named CA-REP-0001 and told me to file the REP request and Rename. The validator report carried real rule IDs (CA-REP-0001, CA-W-7006/7008), a version synced to HC v5.3, and an explicit checked/not_checked coverage list, so I never had to guess what it did and didn't verify. The two-signal validate view — structural PASS beside "HC eValidator: PASS (user attested external)" — left zero doubt about which claim came from where.

Very clear at nearly every step — the validation report gave me actual rule IDs (CA-REP-0001, CA-W-7006/7008) with plain-language messages, so I always knew what was wrong and what to do next. The two-signal split — the structural check passing on its own line while the HC eValidator result sat beside it labelled "user attested external" — was unusually honest and I appreciated not being told the tool did something it didn't. The one thing I'd still have to learn cold is the REP/CESG WebTrader Dossier-ID dance, but the 4-step guidance walked me right through it.

Very clear at each turn — the rule IDs (CA-REP-0001, CA-W-7006/7008) gave me exact language to put in a deviation note, and the 409 export block told me precisely what to fix rather than dumping a broken zip on me. The PDF/A advisories were the one place I briefly worried I'd done something wrong, but the report was explicit that they were advisory-only and that the 5 residual ones belonged to files I uploaded, not files the tool wrote. The enforced-SoD 422 message spelled out signer, author, tenant policy — no guesswork.

This earned real trust because it fails closed — it refused to emit a package while a blocker stood, showed me the finding, then only produced the 11008-byte zip stamped X-Export-Validation=passed after I genuinely fixed it. What matters most to me is the honesty: it repeatedly states it is NOT Health Canada's official eValidator, records my external eValidator PASS as "user_attested_external" rather than claiming parity, and the e-sign verify re-checksums the live leaves for tamper. I would rely on it to get a sequence structurally clean and Part-11 defensible, but I would still run the real eValidator before transmit — which is exactly what the tool tells me to do, and that alignment is why I trust it.

This is the first tool of its kind I'd actually trust, precisely because it refuses to overclaim. It failed closed on the placeholder ID and would not emit a package until validation genuinely passed — that fail-closed behavior is exactly what I need to defend to a client. The enforced segregation-of-duties hard-block (422 when author tries to self-sign under workspace policy), the tamper-evident manifest with live re-verification, and the Part-11 ledger recording sod_policy_source=workspace_policy are all real controls an auditor can replay. Critically, it never pretends to be HC's eValidator; it tells me to run the official one before transmit. That boundary is why I'd rely on it — it's honest about being a pre-flight, not the gate itself.

This earned real trust because it fails closed and is scrupulously honest about scope. It refused to emit a package while validation hadn't passed — no misleading download — and every screen repeats that this is a STRUCTURAL check, NOT HC's eValidator. The eValidator PASS is stored as user_attested_external with the report file and checksum, never a parity self-claim; the e-sign is labeled "Part 11 aligned, not an external certification." That restraint is exactly why I'd rely on it for assembly and pre-flight. My one reservation: it checks structural PDF/A-1b markers and backbone, not full ISO 19005-1 or content adequacy — so it's a strong pre-flight, not a substitute for the actual eValidator run before transmission, which the tool itself tells me.

More than I expected, and specifically because it refuses to overclaim. It fails closed on export, uses real HC rule schemes, and everywhere it draws the hard line: this is a STRUCTURAL check, NOT eValidator — run eValidator before you transmit. That honesty is exactly why I'd trust it as a pre-flight, not a replacement. The enforced SoD hard-block (422, workspace policy, sod_policy_source in the Part-11 ledger) is real Part-11 defensibility, not a checkbox. What it does NOT and openly says it does not do — full ISO 19005-1 PDF/A, content/quality, HC screening — is precisely the stuff I still run my own tools for, so I'd rely on it for assembly and gating, then eValidator for the go/no-go.

This is the part that actually won me over. It refused to hand me a download while validation was failing (the 409), and it only exported after the block genuinely cleared — it wasn't just theatre. And it kept telling me what it is NOT: "this is not Health Canada's official eValidator," the eValidator PASS is user-attested not something it ran, and the e-sign is "Part-11 aligned, not an external certification." As a junior I've been burned by tools that overclaim, so a tool that under-claims and hard-blocks makes me trust it MORE, not less. I would still run the real HC eValidator before transmitting, exactly like it tells me to — which is the correct behaviour.

This is the part that actually won me over. It fails closed — it refused to export sequence 0000 with a placeholder ID (409) and only produced the zip once validation genuinely passed, so it can't quietly hand me a bad package. And it's honest about its own limits: it says plainly it is NOT Health Canada's eValidator, it records my external eValidator PASS as "user-attested" rather than pretending it ran it, and the PDF/A checks stay advisory instead of falsely blocking. The e-signature verify re-checked all 10 leaves for tampering, and the SoD check correctly flagged the author-signs-own-work conflict. For a junior like me that honesty is worth more than a tool that overclaims — I'd trust it to prepare and gate a filing, as long as I still run the real eValidator myself, which it explicitly tells me to.

This is the first tool of this kind I've watched be honest with me, and that earns real trust. It failed closed — refused to emit a package while validation hadn't passed — and only produced the 11KB zip stamped 'passed' once the blocker genuinely cleared; that fail-closed behavior is exactly what my SOPs demand. It repeatedly and prominently says it is NOT Health Canada's eValidator, records my eValidator result as user-attested rather than claiming parity, and labels the e-sign as 'Part-11 aligned, not an external certification.'
